issue_context.title: Make it possible to access specific elements of an X500DistinguishedName
comments: I couldn't figure out the best area label to add to this issue. Please help me learn by adding exactly one [area label](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/area-owners.md).

It seems `AsnEncodedData` has fairly primitive formatting capabilities on non-Windows. The `X500DistinguishedName` type is much better at formatting X500 names, but it doesn't help if you want individual components of the DN.

@bartonjs has there been any thought about a proposal for X500DN to support enumerating the individual components?
Not serious thought, but it probably makes sense.  Of course, if I can ever get AsnReader public then there's a workaround :)
@vcsjones Hopefully the proposal above matches what you expected after our discussion. If not, there's still time to change it.
Well, GetSingleValueValue throws when HasMultipleValues is true, it's only null for OCTET STRING/BIT STRING/OID/etc for a single value.  So the NotNullWhen wouldn't help/be-accurate

> So the NotNullWhen wouldn't help/be-accurate

Ah, right... (backs away in to shrubs)

review_comments:
Can `ReadAnyAsnString` throw a `DecoderFallbackException`?

If it can, should we wrap it, or doc it?
I suppose the idea is to list the ~6-8 common Oids that appear in the RDNs (Eg. Common Name `CN`, Country `C`, Organization `O`, ...)

> I suppose the idea is to list the ~6-8 common Oids that appear in the RDNs.

Sorry, I'm not following.  The comment suggests that the whole method implementation is ifdef'd out purely because of the inability to use list patterns, which appear to only be used in one place that's easily replaceable with something that does work.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72235#discussion_r921721562

The idea is to avoid allocations for the common values I think.

This file is used in two main places: System.Security.Cryptography.dll (shared runtime, NetCoreAppCurrent) and System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs (OOB, includes a netstandard2.0 target, a ns2.1 target, some netcoreapp targets, and netfx).

Given how broad a TFM set it builds with, I doubt anyone is even running the netstandard2.0 build, but it makes the package complete for the ns2.0 ref.  The netfx build is mostly a facade to GAC:System.Security.dll, but there are probably a few common OIDs that could get added to the `#else` block as we start moving things from `AsnReader.ReadObjectIdentifier()` to a "your bytes look familiar, here's the answer" approach.

In the medium to long term, I'd expect most (if not all) of the shared OIDs in this file to be represented in the pattern-match, most of which aren't relevant to the parts of the Pkcs library that aren't typeforwards on .NET Framework.  So it's really a question of overall best-fit:

* Use the list pattern for newer targets, ignore the old ones as low usage.
* Use the list pattern for newer targets, add some tracing in the `#else` and add ones that get hit running PKCS7 tests on netfx.
* Use the expanded form everywhere.
* Keep doing what we've been doing (full data interpretation and building new System.String instances for every call to ReadObjectIdentifier)

I started with expanded, then @vcsjones showed me the list pattern, and I thought it read better, so I'm at 1 with an easy future pivot to 2.  But I'm definitely willing to be convinced to go with 3 or 4.

If the method is just an optimization and we don't think that optimization matters in the few to none cases where it'll be used downlevel, seems fine to just leave the code as-is.  It just seemed that there was this long method, seemingly important, and entirely commented out if a language feature wasn't available to just save a few lines of code.

```diff
 #else
-            // Cannot use list patterns on older TFMs.
+            // The list pattern isn't available in System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs for the
+            // netstandard2.0 or netfx builds.  Any OIDs that it's important to optimize in
+            // those contexts can be matched on here, but using a longer form of matching.
+
             return null;
 #endif
```

Better?
If this is true, how do you get at the elements?

You need to go back to `AsnReader` and read the distinguished name yourself. This is an exceedingly rare scenario, but one that needs to be guarded against nonetheless. Multi-value RDNs are (probably) going to get banned in WebPKI in the near future.

This took me a minute to understand what is going on. This is just avoiding an allocation while trying to spin through the RDN while consuming the OID, correct?

Maybe this is worth a comment. Alternatively, I guess you could just peek the tag, check it, and consume the value.
